questions.question: Why does ordinary pixel-by-pixel image autoregression struggle with a 2D image grid?
options: It cannot represent images as discrete tokens
It must commit in a 1D order before seeing later context
It requires a diffusion schedule for every pixel
It predicts all pixels at one resolution in parallel
questions.explanation: Pixel autoregression flattens a 2D grid into a raster sequence, so early positions must be chosen before the model sees later spatial context. VAR instead predicts a whole resolution scale at once and advances from coarse to fine.

questions.question: What does each VAR scale encode in its residual VQ tokenizer?
options: A single global text embedding for the prompt
The class label of the final image
The residual left by earlier, coarser scales
An independent full copy of the original image
questions.explanation: Each scale tokenizes the residual left after reconstructing earlier scales; the decoder sums upsampled scale embeddings to recover the latent features. Independent full-image copies would repeat the same information instead of refining it.

questions.question: Within one scale, how are VAR tokens generated?
options: Each position is predicted one after another
Only the top-left token is predicted at each pass
All positions are predicted in parallel
Positions are generated by a reverse diffusion chain
questions.explanation: VAR is causal across scales, but all spatial positions at a given scale are predicted in parallel. Predicting each position one after another would reintroduce the raster-order bottleneck the scale structure avoids.

questions.question: If a VAR model uses K=10 scales, how many transformer passes does generation require?
options: 100 passes, ten per scale
10 times the number of pixels
1 pass, one for each image pixel
10 passes, one for each scale
questions.explanation: Generation makes one transformer pass per scale, so K=10 requires 10 passes; the number of positions within each scale does not add passes because that scale is predicted in parallel.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts VAR’s iteration axis with diffusion’s?
options: Both generate all resolutions in one pass
VAR removes noise; diffusion adds resolution
VAR adds resolution; diffusion removes noise
Both iterate over pixel raster positions
questions.explanation: VAR iterates by adding finer spatial resolution, while diffusion iterates by removing noise from a sample. They decompose generation along different axes rather than both applying the same denoising sequence.

questions.question: A coarse image layout should be fixed before fine details are generated. Which VAR property supports this?
options: Every scale is sampled independently from noise
The finest scale is generated before the summary
Later scales condition on all earlier scales
Tokens within every scale use raster causality
questions.explanation: Later scales receive all previous-scale tokens as context, letting the coarse layout constrain finer details. Sampling each scale independently would remove the hierarchical dependency needed to keep details aligned with the layout.
